article.title: Impressions (October 2026)
article.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
article.content: Impressions is where ROC DSA members can share what they’re reading, listening to, viewing, or otherwise experiencing. If you have two hundred words about the culture at large you’d like to share with your comrades, submit to Rich J on Slack or to the Red Star at steering@rocdsa.org . Trans, Punk, and Somehow Legal? Abigail J watched: The People’s Joker I recently stumbled upon what is easily one of my new top 5 movies, The People’s Joker by Vera Drew (2022). This movie is an insane transgender coming of age story set in an unofficial DC Comics universe and presented in a psychedelic mixed media format (complete with live action, stop motion, and 2-D animation). The production and editing were completely crowd-sourced, and I’m genuinely not sure how this legally got made. As a (very recently out) trans woman, this movie hit me in a way that almost no other movie or show has before. During production, this movie morphed from simply being a compilation of Batman satires to a semi-autobiographical narrative of Vera Drew’s life and transition up to that point (the creator and main star). While my story has definitely been different than both Vera’s and the ritual People’s Joker’s, I finally saw aspects of my life represented on film that I had never seen before, and connected to on a visceral level. How would my life be different if I’d seen this five, ten, fifteen years ago? I’ll never know, but I hope some not-yet-aware trans teens get as much (or more) out of this movie than I did. For those interested, the film is available for free at: www.thepeoplesjoker.com Real Americans Isabella D watched: The Americans Elizabeth and Philip Jennings are the quintessential family in Reagan’s America — two kids, a nice house in the suburbs, respectable careers. Their neighbors, and certainly not the affable FBI agent across the street, would never suspect that the two are KGB spies, committing gruesome acts of espionage to tip the scales of the Cold War in the Soviet Union’s favor. Over the course of six seasons, audiences suffer Breaking Bad-esque tension over if and when the Jennings will be found out in The Americans . I mostly enjoyed the series, but with a disclaimer: while the show is a well-crafted drama with four Emmys under its belt, the acute viewer may discern the tint of anti-Communist, pro-western ideals. This gripe is not just paranoia; the creator and showrunner Joe Weisberg is a Reagan-admiring former CIA agent. The Jennings are depicted as destroying themselves for a vague cause, their Marxist convictions never fully elucidated, and dogmatically resisting the prosperous American way of life for an oppressive, decadent Soviet Union. The cinematographic dichotomy alone relays this bias — the US is colorful, vibrant, abundant, and the USSR bleak, dismal, and bureaucratically stifling. To give credit where credit is due, the narrative imparts a great deal of empathy and relatability to Elizabeth and Philip as Soviet illegals before a predominantly western audience. The couple’s dynamic is deeply compelling, tempering my ideological frustration with the show, but the narrative is dragged down by clunky plotlines and a clear predilection for the American way. Rooting for the Underdog. Greg LH watched: Coyote vs. ACME In Coyote vs. ACME , our ever-floundering Wile E. Coyote, and his billboard lawyer Kevin Avery (Will Forte), become the face of underdogs confronting the corporate behemoth ACME over the thousands of malfunctioning products sold to the Coyote. Coyote vs. ACME has a convoluted production history – In 2023 Warner Bros. shelved the fully-made film to obtain a $30 million tax write-off. The film was only released in 2026 following backlash and its subsequent purchase by another production company. On opening day at The Little Theater, Dan Sendker, author of Dance of the Comedians – 75 Years of the Road Runner and Wile E. Coyote gave this context prior to the showing, echoing the content of the film and highlighting the perverted incentives of capitalism. The film delivers the laughs and delights of the original cartoon, with the fun element of live-action overlap. A tale of the little guy going after the corporate behemoth, the Coyote manages to poke his snout at corporate malfeasance. But his revenge is individualistic – there is no moment of organized unity with the other injured members of his class (of cartoon characters). I was hoping for a class action lawsuit, at least. A montage of FBI arrests also places the ideology of the movie within the Mueller-led resistance of Trump One. Don’t think about it too deeply though, just go have a good time.
